title: TENDINITIS, BEGONE! [Healing Tendinopathy / Tendon Pain Rehab for Lifters]
summary: NH's anti-tendinitis guide: tendinitis is a spectrum of tendon inflammation caused by how you move, and it heals through smart movement, never through rest or anti-inflammatories. He explains how to use pain as a guide, find pain-free angles and variations, train in the warm 'valley' between inactivity and re-aggravation, and use ice after training as a minor aid.
claims: Tendinitis is the most common lifting injury and the main reason lifters miss gym time outside of life events
Tendinitis is a spectrum from mild occasional tendon pain to acute inflammation that hurts even at rest and can end in rupture
Tendinitis is caused by movement, but stopping movement is the worst response because immobility aggravates it
Diet-driven inflammation is systemic and has only a minor effect on tendon inflammation; the movement side matters far more
Stress, poor sleep and badly managed rest in the program can cause or aggravate tendinitis, so fix the environment around the tendon before rehabbing it
Muscles are built to break down and rebuild; tendons are built to be very resistant but recover poorly, so tendon wear must be minimized
Soreness is the body saying a muscle is fatigued; tendon pain is a real alarm because the body cannot rebuild tendons quickly
Stopping training atrophies the muscle that shares the tendon's load, so you come back to even worse tendinitis
Tendons get very little blood flow; a pump matters more for tendon health than for muscle growth
An inflamed tendon is not a destroyed tendon; immobilizing it for weeks 'fossilizes' it and leaves you worse off
Take at most one or two days off if the pain is bad, so you don't build a fearful association between the movement and pain
No tendinitis has ever truly healed through rest; it only seems to and then returns because the cause never changed
Taking three to four weeks off is far too long: the tendon loses blood flow, the muscle atrophies and the tendinitis comes back harder
General practitioners know little about physical activity and wrongly prescribe rest and painkillers that only treat symptoms
Avoid anti-inflammatory drugs and painkillers: they mask the pain signal you need for rehab, and anti-inflammatories weaken tendons and promote tears
Post-training tendon inflammation is normal and adaptive; tendinitis is just how much inflammation you cause, so blocking it removes the tendon's ability to adapt
A powerlifter with hip tendinitis squatted on painkillers until his hip gave out and he tore his labrum
Identify exactly which movements cause pain in which tendon, then find variations that still work the muscle with little tendon tension and no pain
Warm-up blood flow reduces tendinitis pain, but if pain returns mid-session you are re-aggravating it and must stop
Train in the 'valley' between inactive moderate pain and acute pain; repeated sessions there widen the pain-free window until the tendinitis is gone
Tendinitis is a game of angles: change the joint angle until a variation is painless, e.g. skull crushers may hurt while bar triceps extensions don't
If any elbow flexion or extension hurts, the tendinitis is severe and the pain-free window is tiny, so rehab will take a long time
Reintroduce the painful movement with no load to regain function; if it always hurts, ban it, since any movement has many equally good alternatives
NH had tendinitis in both knees (acute in the left) and both elbows for years and is now completely pain-free after rehabbing properly
End the workout right before pain becomes acute; the pain is a warning that the tendon could rupture
Lifters who tear a biceps tendon have usually ignored biceps tendinitis for months
A natural lifting conservative loads with no tendinitis will not have a tendon snap unless he ego-lifts
NH lifts very heavy on biceps exercises and has never had biceps tendinitis or injury
Don't power through tendinitis once warm; train around the pain so you can eventually train without pain
Don't overreact by stopping training or underreact by ignoring the pain, and don't stay at low effort forever or the muscle won't progress
Icing helps reduce inflammation without drugs, but it won't cure tendinitis
For acute tendinitis, let the tendon cool after training, then apply a wrapped ice pack for 10-15 minutes, stay still, and only move slowly about 10 minutes later
Only corrective exercise that stresses the tendon enough to adapt ends tendinitis for good
